utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Sureta Chana, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, myself, and case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. President. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, on behalf of Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom. Today we will continue with the examination of an archivist, and we will then be examining a second archivist. So the agenda will be quite full given the questions we have for these two witnesses. Could the usher call the witness who testified yesterday into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Major. I would first like to check that you are receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. Yes, I am receiving the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now continue with the cross-examination. The Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Omerkic.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the day yesterday we discussed that fact that the Prosecution took from the archives of Bosnia and Hercegovina in October 2000 several thousand documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many documents they took exactly. A list has been made. We had a list here of all the material issued. We had this list yesterday, and I think that it is correct. It was a list of the material issued in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And yesterday, you said that the greatest number of documents were taken from the archives in a military facility in Konjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Konjic is 70 kilometres south of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Other documents were taken from the Ramiz Salcin barracks in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was before Konjic. These documents were taken from those archives in the Ramiz Salcin barracks before Konjic. And then after some time had elapsed, documents were taken from Konjic, too, as we moved to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also said that investigators took entire binders from the archives in Konjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases, too. They took what they were interested in. They were given access to whatever they thought was necessary. I know that they took an entire binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, please tell me whether this search in Konjic was carried out during the day or at night?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day. During working hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After they had taken those documents away, the investigators made a list of them, and they provided you with this list?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as they took either an individual document or, for example, an entire binder, they would make a note of it. I was present at all times as well as my colleagues. We would always make a record of this. We would say the 1st Corps commander issued an order in 1996 that concerned a given document or a number of documents, and we would make a list. We would make a record of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me whether the search for documents in the Ramiz Salcin barracks was carried out during the day or at night?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Ramiz Salcin barracks, it's possible that it was carried out during the day, but also at night. That's quite correct. I know that I was there, and the representative from the ministry because it was a lot of work. All the material in the Ramiz Salcin barracks had to be photocopied immediately by us because they asked for a lot of documents. We had a lot of work to do. So they took documents from Konjic and then kept them here in this Tribunal as they saw there were a lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Original documents were taken from Konjic; documents weren't photocopied in Konjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The documents from the Ramiz Salcin barracks were -- some of them were photocopied, and others were originals that were taken away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More documents -- when they took a lot of documents from the Ramiz Salcin barracks, in such cases I think that all the original material they requested was material that they photocopied, and then we made a list of these documents. I don't think that they took any originals on that occasion from the Ramiz Salcin barracks, whereas in Konjic they only took originals. They didn't photocopy any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Ramiz Salcin barracks, were you also present when the documents were listed, or were you subsequently provided with a list of the documents for you to check and certify?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever was provided to these people, to the Tribunal, a record was made of this immediately on the spot. It was typed out. I was present, and when the list was compiled I would sign it as the chief of the archives, the representative of the Tribunal and the representative of the ministry - Eremisic [phoen] was his name at the time - signed this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness a document shown to him by the Prosecution. 01062519 is the number of the document, and it is a certificate of documents taken from the archives. And a list of the documents taken. If the Registry doesn't have this document, I have a copy that the Prosecution showed to the witness yesterday. So could the witness please be shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at it and then place it on the ELMO so that everyone else in the courtroom can see the same document. You should now be able to see the document on your screen. My colleague from the Prosecution showed you this document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You recognised your signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is obvious that this document is in English.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know English? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You signed the English document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the first sentence -- yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, in the archives, there is a translation into the Bosnian language of this document. So I also signed the Bosnian version of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since in the second line it says that these documents were taken from the archives located at the Ramiz Salcin barracks in Sarajevo, this is one of the lists of documents that on the 12th and 13th of October were taken from this location.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the last page of this document. At the top, the number is 01062526. That's the Prosecution's number. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the numbers in the first column mean. It says "document number" at the top. What do the documents in the first column represent? What do the numbers in the first column represent?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first column?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A hundred thousand and something.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And 47. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What does that represent?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it represents a binder or a binder that contained --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My question is do you know what this number is? Is that a number used in the archives? Was that a number that came from the Prosecution, or is it some other number the meaning of which is unknown to you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number is the number of the list typed out. The Tribunal representative did this. For example, let's say it says the 1st Corps here. That's its number. That must be his number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you know what this number is, what it means? It's not an archives' number, it's not a number from the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina? It's a number that was typed out by the person who was taking away the documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last column, is it a column that refers to the description of the documents that are being taken? At the top, it says "description of documents". Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under that column, it mentioned the unit this material came from. It's, in fact, a binder or some of the material from one binder. I can't see this very clearly. I can't see which unit is referred to, but for example, it says the 1st Corps Command, and then it mentions the year. It says 1992-1993 here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's important to know that it's a description of these documents --

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then it continues to refer to the units, whether they're from Zenica or Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So under this column we should have a list of all the documents that were taken from the archive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Documents from one binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in all the columns, we'll have references to all documents taken away?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the third line now. Here it says that it is a binder containing documents from the year 1992. Group 1, the supreme command staff, the security services administration, and a report is mentioned. And at the end, we have a number, 61. There's also the date, the 16th of May. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what this number means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at number 5 now. It says the 13th of October, 2000, and then it goes on. The binder contains documents from 1992, 1993. Group 1. The Bugojno municipal staff combat reports from the 22nd of July 1992 to 24th of September 1993. And then we have the number 140. Does this mean that there were 140 documents in this binder?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. But again, I'm not sure. It's possible that the Tribunal wasn't interested in the entire binder. Perhaps they only took 60 or 140 documents from a given binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the their one from below, the 13th of October. It says that the document concerns the year 1993. It says the corps is the third one; the unit is KD. An order from the 4th -- from 413 up until 3, and then you don't see the other number. Does that mean that these are documents that the Prosecution took?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate line, it says that the documents contained in the binder are from 1993. It's group 1, the 3rd Corps. The command units orders. The date is from the 9th of January up until the 10th of May, and the number is 314. It's mentioned 314 documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the last line for 1993, we have a binder from the 3rd Corps. I won't read everything out. It says from the 5th of January until the 24th of July, and we would have 426 documents in this binder. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably a record of how many documents were provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this document, I didn't sign any other document that might describe each of these 426 documents individually. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite possible because that's a huge amount of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So they took entire binders, and you just signed that you had handed over documents with a certain -- binders with a certain number of documents, but you didn't sign for having handed over individual documents?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each binder had a list of the documents, of the original documents. At that time, we probably thought - I always consulted with the representative from the Ministry of Defence who was a constant link between me as the chief, the Tribunal, the army, the Ministry of Defence, et cetera - and that was probably the best way to hand over archival material.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm not at all criticising you. I just want to know whether you handed over documents to the Tribunal in complete binders, and you only noted the name of the binder and the number of documents contained in the binder.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't make a list of individual documents as there were tens of thousands of documents, and the work involved would have been immense. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the original documents were brought to The Hague, in fact, you left without any documents in the archives. All you had were these receipts. I've shown you an example of such receipts.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution kept for one year those documents and returned you copies of the originals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned the copies of the originals, you could only compare these documents with these receipts. You could only check to see whether there were a sufficient number of binders and whether each binder contained a sufficient number of documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They returned all the originals, but only -- they returned photocopies of the originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't have a document that would allow you to make a comparison, that would allow you to check that each of these 426 documents were there. All you could check was that there were 426 documents.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had photocopied lists. We didn't photocopy each document. But Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we had a list of all the orders from one binder, from one box. So we knew what we had to search for if it was necessary. We knew where these documents were located. We had our security service which also controlled these operations, and everyone suggested that this is how we should work. And there was no other way to proceed. There was no other possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omerkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence team, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At this point in time, Ms. Benjamin, do you have any additional questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, I have a number of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, yesterday, you said that when the investigators arrived, you were in contact with your superior. I would like you to tell me who your superior was in the Ministry of Defence. You said the commander, but who was he? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I expressed myself well, but I'll try to clarify this now. When I mentioned the commander, I wanted to say that I worked as a soldier, as an officer, under the orders of the commander. And it was my duty to work in such a way independently of the Tribunal's attitude. The attitude of my superiors was, the political view in Bosnia was also, that it was necessary to be particularly open when cooperating with the Tribunal. So it was quite clearly -- I was quite clearly told from my -- by my commanders that this is how I was to work, although I personally never actually met the commander. But we knew each other, but they probably wouldn't have recognised me if we had met. But it's not as if orders were issued at all times. But an order would arrive, and an order would say "for the needs of the International Tribunal in The Hague, it's necessary to issue such and such a document." Well, what I want to say is that I received orders. For example, the Tribunal would ask for a document, and then they would ask us for a document on a second occasion, and we would do all we could to find the document but we couldn't find the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is precise. What is your commander's name?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of my first commander was General Rasim Delic. He was my superior in the archives. He was a well-known general in the army. After him, it was General Dudakovic. And both acted as I have described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that you, who are the chief of the archives in the army, between you and your superior, the only person above you was either General Delic or General Dudakovic. There was no one else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the person I did have some kind of direct contact with was someone from the Ministry of Defence who was in civilian clothes, but he held the rank of major. It was in the Ministry of Defence. I think that the political view, of the view of the Presidency and the military authorities was that he should establish contact and say, Adem, this is how you should proceed. Our age was similar. We held a similar rank. So when material was handed over to the Tribunal, he would also sign for this. And this seemed to be logical to me. So I didn't have direct contact with the commander. It's not as if he told me what had to be done, but first of all we would receive something in writing, and then this person from the ministry would establish contact. It was an officer. I don't know what his duties were. Perhaps he was involved in security or communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the investigators arrived, you signed the documents -- a document that the Defence showed you. Your name is on the document, but also the name of Commander Ramesic Suad.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suad Ramesic is not a commander. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what rank did he hold?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He held the rank of major. So we held the same rank. We were the executive organ, so to speak. He performed his duties in the sense of establishing contact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he worked with you or did he have an office somewhere else, Major Suad Ramezic.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had an office in the Ministry of Defence. That's where the Ministry of Defence is located now. That's where he had an office. When Tribunal representatives arrived, he was always present. He controlled things to make sure that nothing went wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now we have a clearer view of this. When you assumed your duties in 1995, when you arrived in this building where the archives were already located, could you confirm that archival material had already arrived there, but you weren't aware of how this material had arrived there?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were documents in boxes which hadn't been processed. Later on, among those documents, we found some very important documents for this Tribunal which we later processed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, I listened to you carefully, and at a certain point you said that there were three other persons working with you, one of whom was a woman --

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you were the only man with three women. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, there was another lady, but she retired later. Or she left anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you were four in all. Before the investigators came, and they came in October because this operation took place in October 2000, before they came, were there any other persons who came to consult the archives? And if so, who gave them the authorisation to do that?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Konjic, before this seizure of large quantities, representatives of the Tribunal came earlier on as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Representatives of the Tribunal. But were there any other persons, officers, investigators, university professors, or others? Did any other people come to look at the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A component part of our duties was to lend archival material to people in Bosnia who were in the army preparing reports or monographs about various events during the war. And it was our duty to give them these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When those people came, they had authorisation issued by whom? Was it by the Defence Ministry or by you? Who granted them this authorisation.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before they would come, we would receive an order from the commander. This was only an order. These were very high-ranking officers. But only an order from the commander of the BH Army would come to me, and only once I had such an order could I, through the Ministry of Defence, we would receive a document from the army commander saying that on such and such a day, such and such a person, first and last name, rank, would come looking for certain documents from a certain period. And when we received such a document, then we prepare the material requested if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm understanding you properly, between 1995 and 2000, before the investigators came, you're telling us that army commanders of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, or 4th Corps would send people to look at the archives with the authorisation of the Defence Ministry? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this: I can't quite interpret things like that. But I wish to say in this Tribunal, that whatever I did, I did following orders of the commander of the army. And if someone was coming from the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd Corps, the commander of the army would inform me that such and such a person would be coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So when this person arrived, would he show you an ID card, and did you have a book in which you registered the arrival of this person who came to consult the archives?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we receive the document from the command, and when the date mentioned in the order comes, and if one of these people arrives, then he gets a copy of that same document, and he shows us this, and we say "we have the same document. Everything is fine." And then we act as ordered. If we're unable to find something, then we ask him what it is he needs. At the end, we would note down what document we gave him, and he would sign it and I would sign it. But they were under the obligation to return these documents to us within one month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I'm touching on a question that has escaped the attention of many. You're telling us that people who came took documents, left with those documents, and then returned them to you later on?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they took documents, they could only take photocopies. For instance, the monograph of a particular brigade is in preparation. And they're looking for reports from 1992, 1993, et cetera. And then a list is made of what they need for this monograph. Then we bring the original documents, and he says, "yes, that's the document I'm looking for." But we don't give him the original. We photocopy it on our own photocopying machine and give him the photocopy, and he has to sign a document saying that we have given him a photocopy of an original document which we kept in the archives. But even those photocopies, they had to return to us after a month or so, just in case there could be some sort of abuse or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the investigators came in 2000, did other people come to look at the documents that had been looked at by the investigators?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anyone came specifically to check the material. At least for as long as I was there. I have to note that 2001, I was transferred to another position. And from then on, I had nothing to do with the archives. But while I was there, I don't think that anyone checked on the documents given to the Tribunal. I don't think so, nor was it possible to do that because the system was such as it was. He would have to go to the commander and then the commander would have to give me the appropriate order. Though I was of a low rank, I was very wary in allowing access to the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that the archives were in certain rooms and that the brigade or army corps also had places to keep documents. Regarding the 7th Muslim Brigade, you know what the 7th Muslim Brigade is?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of it. I don't know particularly what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The archives of the 7th Muslim Brigade, where were they?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our command, there was a significant quantity of archival material belonging to the 7th Muslim Brigade. I don't know how much, but a considerable amount of documents of all kinds, orders, commands, reports, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to the best of your knowledge, the archives of the 7th Brigade, were they frequently consulted?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Tribunal looked at those documents most. I don't think there was a great deal of viewing of archival documents. We were really somehow -- I can't say barricaded in, but we wouldn't allow archival material to be taken away easily. I know that when these monographs of particular brigades were prepared, then all the brigades would come from time to time. But I don't think that this particular brigade was very much in demand. But there were individual cases when the Tribunal - I don't know why - a person might come looking for a particular set of documents. But not so much. With the exception of these large seizures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The national courts, the courts of your country, would the judges or investigators of those courts come to look at the archives? Or was it only investigators of The Hague Tribunal? Were there other investigators linked to your national courts that would come to consult the archives as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that some judges would request certain documents from us. And there were not so many instances of this, but they didn't like our system because our response would be that they would address themselves to the commander, and then the commander would send an order to us. So that is how we proceeded, through written documents. They never sent us a representative of the Hague Tribunal without a written document reaching us first. I don't remember, but there were some demand, and we did our best to meet those demands by indicating what the proper procedure was. They had to respect the procedure and go through the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. I'm going to show you now a document. It is 301 on the Prosecution list. You will see it is an order. I won't enter into the substance of that order because it is in B/C/S. I just wish you to comment on the markings on this document. You will see that there are numbers on it, so I would like to ask the usher to put this document under the ELMO. You see this document. In the left, there are two numbers encircled. 2022. We see two numbers. 2022 with a circle around it. And 622 encircled. Who wrote those numbers?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it be clearer, please. It's what I was saying yesterday. I don't know whether this is my handwriting. In an ordinary pencil, I would write down this number. We would on our own initiative write this down in pencil so that we could later rub it out if necessary in order to classify documents. For instance, if this 622, if I wrote down that number and the document didn't come from the main command, it was not processed in the main command archive, the other one written in, 2022, is clearly a sign that someone in a lower-level unit had been working on it and who classified it in his own way. He didn't really classify it at all. He just put together reports and orders and all kinds of things, and obviously this list of his was much bigger. So we see the number 2022, whereas 622 is probably -- means that it was a document belonging to the fourth group, which was a large one, but not a very significant one. I told our assistant that if you write down numbers, do it in pencil so that we can rub it out easily. And this other one in marker, I don't think was done in our archives but in a lower-level unit where they had a big pile of all sorts of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President. Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying on the right, there's S/R0182/140613/891 -- 1991. Who could have written down these numbers?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, we didn't pay much attention to these numbers. But clearly, they are an administrative numbering of the unit in question. Sometimes it was kind of an identification number. When we didn't know which group to put it in, then we would try to decipher where it came from. But this is obviously from the administrative archive that registered the document for the first time. I must say this is confusing. I don't know what it is at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see at the bottom, there's a blue stamp. And this type of stamp, was it the official stamp used in the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that was so. Each large unit had its own stamp Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the corps level down to the brigade level. I don't know whether any battalion had a stamp. Maybe a military police battalion. Larger units had their own stamps with our coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please turn the document over. You see that on the back, there are markings as well. There's a large stamp in blue, and we see the word "korpus" with a number. Then Predato in circles, and then a date, an hour. This type of stamp, did you see such stamps frequently?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I would interpret this as being the archival stamp. Or if this document was drawn up in a particular brigade, and then we see this number up here, they didn't have this square stamp, then they just wrote down the protocol number or archival number. And then when it reached a higher level, 3rd Corps, for instance, the corps had its own stamp. So they had a stamp, and in this stamp, the orderly number was written, and everything else. So I assume that this document came from a lower-level unit to the 3rd Corps command as the superior command, and I would say that this is quite customary. I'm not surprised by anything I see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Usher, will you pick up the document, please. And I'm coming to the end of my questions. I will show you another document that you were shown yesterday. And this is Exhibit 132 which you will also place under the ELMO. I'm sorry, 133. Look at this document, please. Yesterday, the Defence asked you some questions about it saying that it was not signed. Will you please look at the top of this document, the top, please. You see that there is a line, and I see in B/C/S the word "kripto." Was this document a document sent to be encrypted?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. We considered this to be an element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you will agree with me that it is not signed. When you're encrypting a document, you don't sign it. You never encrypt a signature. That never happens, does it? When a document is encrypted, and "kripto" is indicated, the arrival of that document must be indicated the date and the hour when the document was decrypted. I see here that this document was sent on the 26th of January 1993, and it was probably decrypted on the 27th of January at 0021 hours. Would that be the way to interpret this document? I must remind you, after all, you were a major, an officer.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would be my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 26th of January is the date when the document was drafted, the time when the time was issued. The 27th, the document may have been written today but perhaps the commander was not there to sign it or for some other reason it wasn't urgent, and then they sent it the next day on the 27th. So the date is not at all important, the 26th or the 27th. For me, that is the same. It would happen often that we would have a document on the 26th, and it would be sent on the 28th, particularly if a weekend intervenes. For instance, it may be written on a Friday and sent on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, the person sending the document, the encryptor, the person that we see initialed on the right-hand side, it says "obradio" in B/C/S, is that the person in charge of encrypting the document? You can see a signature in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What does obradio mean in English.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say that I assume that that is the signature of the person working on the encrypting though I personally never had any contact with those people so I don't know how they work. So it is only an assumption on our part -- on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So when this document is encrypted and needs to be decrypted by an electronic system and received, would they then have a stamp on it, a stamp of arrival? Is that the one we see in the middle which says "Sarajevo, the 2nd of October - 291"? Would that be the arrival stamp in the middle of the document?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this stamp is again the square stamp that every larger unit or brigade had. So it's an administrative stamp. And we see it says "Defence Ministry" here. And we personally considered such stamps as an element of authenticity. Now, how it was put there, I didn't enter into that. We did our best to collect all the indications that we needed for our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My very last question is why these documents which were archived, why no one had the idea of putting on them an archive stamp with a signature of the person in charge of the archives, yourself, which would indicate that such a document has been archived? Why isn't there any archive stamp on these documents? Why didn't you have this idea to suggest to your superior general that all these documents needed to be stamped by the archives, needed to have an archive stamp on them?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many ideas and proposals on my own part based on my experience and work in the archives that I addressed to my superior commands. However, some suggestions were adopted; others were not. Why this wasn't, my simple explanation would be that probably -- actually, what they had in mind, I don't know. But deep down, I did believe that we needed something like that. And I did have some proposals. But I didn't insist too much because out of modesty, I would say I feared that my superiors might say "you want to have a stamp to be able to sign yourself" so that I had to carry every document to my boss for him to sign, and then that document would be put under the command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this would add to the importance of the archives, and also to the chief of the archives. But out of modesty, I didn't want to put any pressure on them because I was more of a manual worker over there. Why they didn't do that, I don't know. It would require certain personnel changes probably. Anyway, it's perhaps beyond my terms of reference, nor am I able to give you a proper answer. Because only high-level military units were entitled to stamps, brigades, corps. I was chief of the archives and of the library. So...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But didn't you believe that you, too, were important, the best evidence of that is that you are in the Tribunal now. Don't you think that you had the responsibility to inform your hierarchy of the fact that these documents should be stamped by the archives? Did you write any written reports suggesting and conveying these ideas that you have been mentioning?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but there were some generalised proposals on our part regarding the organisational structure of the library and archives. There was a joint command of the federation army where there was the Bosniak and the Croatian component together. And within such general documents, we would indicate that that might be necessary. But I can't remember now. I would talk about this with my immediate superior. What I did insist upon was that they facilitate our work or modernise the work of the archives. And as the years passed after the war, we felt that we could be provided with the more modern technical resources and devices to deal with the archives. But we were treated as a small segment, a small sector within the main command which had its own stamp. Maybe I wasn't aware of the importance myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Are there any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the part of the Defence, no questions. On the part of the Prosecution, no questions. In that case, Major, thank you. You have completed your testimony here. We thank you for coming to The Hague, for having answered all the questions of all the parties, for trying to explain to the Judges your work in the archives, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and the problems connected with the preservation of these documents. Thank you. And we wish you a safe journey home, and best wishes hoping that your postgraduate studies will be completed successfully so that you can continue your career because you told us that you are in early retirement, but we hope you will have occasion to become active again. So we thank you very much. And I'll ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin, I believe you have a second archivist who will be called to be heard as a witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But this is not an archivist. This is more like a data-entry recorder clerk. And if I may inform the Trial Chamber, if I'm so allowed, Mr. President, in my mission a week ago, if we look at Prosecution Exhibit 133, which is the one that I indicated to the witness while he was on the stand, we would see the name Major Ramezic Suad appearing all the time. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, those people were liaison officers, they came from the ministry, and they just came to assist the Tribunals when they were doing the search. In fact, we interviewed six people, and out of the six only two, this gentleman and the one who's to come next, had anything about or knew anything about archives. Since I'm on that point, my colleague at this moment is also interviewing somebody who we just discovered with some 30 years of experience of archiving, so we would probably have her come in next week. And with respect to Prosecution Exhibit 301, if I could just draw your attention to the fact that the number 0182-1461, which was also written by hand, is a Prosecution number, it's an ERN number, and I'm told that the repeated number in handwriting came from the evidence unit. So those numbers derived out of the Prosecution. Yes, we have the second witness now, Smriko Sabahudin, who is a data clerk. And my colleague, Sureta Chana, will be taking that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the usher to call this witness into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. I would first like to check that you are receiving interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution to testify about technical matters that concern the archives. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you please tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Sabahudin Smriko. I was born on the 3rd of February 1964.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which town or village were you born in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a professional member of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a lieutenant first-class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what position did you hold in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, I was involved in the delivery of mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a civilian or a member of the military in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which unit were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before 1993, I was the member of the 1st Zenica Detachment. It was a territorial unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before 1993 and during the year 1993, where were you? During 1993, from January to December, where were you on duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 1st of April, I was in the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were a member of the 7th Muslim Brigade. And what did you do in the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was involved in the delivery of the mail to other units within the brigade. We delivered documents to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were in a certain sense the postman who would deliver the 7th Brigade mail to other units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a military term for such a postman. I'm not sure what it is in your language. But that is what you were? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was the deliverer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You were the dispatcher. That's an English term, but why not. You'll take the solemn declaration. Could you please read out the text that you will be shown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed here. You will first have to answer questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution, who are to your right. And the person sitting in the middle will be examining you. After this stage has been completed, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will also ask you questions. This is what we call the cross-examination. This is the common-law term. After these questions have been put to you, the Prosecution can ask you additional questions. The three Judges sitting before you may at any point in time put questions to you, but as a rule we prefer to wait for the end of the examination and cross-examination, and the Judges will certainly put questions to you. If a question appears to be complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it because we expect your answers to be clear and precise. If a question is too complex, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you should naturally not lie because if you give false testimony you could end up in prison. A witness could be fined or given a prison sentence of up to seven years. The Trial Chamber informs witnesses of this possibility if false testimony is given. And there is another element, another factor I would like to mention, but it shouldn't be applicable to you. When a witness answers a question, if a witness doesn't want to answer a question because he believes that this could be -- his answer could be used against him, in such a case the witness may refuse to answer the question. In such a case, the Trial Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question but guarantees the witness a form of immunity. I'll now turn to the second thing I wanted to tell you. As you said that you were a former 7th Muslim Brigade soldier, we won't be asking you questions about the 7th Muslim Brigade, about what the 7th Muslim Brigade did. You are a witness who is here to testify about technical issues, and you will only be answering technical questions about documents. We won't be dealing with what the 7th Muslim Brigade actually did. We'll be dealing with purely technical issues. So it is the Trial Chamber's opinion that you will only be answering technical questions about the work that you were involved in. Have you understood everything that I have said? If so, say "da."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've understood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to the Prosecution. They have 15 minutes because we'll have to have the break very soon. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With the Court's permission, I will lead the witness on certain nonessential particulars and employment history.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you please give your full name for to Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's already been done. So it's not necessary to put questions to the witness that have already been put to him. We've already asked him to inform us of his identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just thought for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You're currently serving as a military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when a Judge asks a witness to inform us of his identity, his name appears in the transcript. So it's already into the record. If you want to do this again, why not, but that would be a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You're serving as a military officer in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: As a junior officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to speak more loudly so that we can hear your voice, so that we can hear your answers. Please speak loudly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a junior officer, not an officer. I was a noncommissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I was a sergeant first-class.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are you stationed in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you're involved in administration duties as a chief of general services. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were educated in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At the administrative school, secondary-school level. Right?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You obtained a diploma in administration as a qualified administration technician. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At 18 years of age, you performed compulsory military service in the Yugoslav National Army, the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And that would be from October 1982 until December 1983?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, following your military service, you were unemployed until 1986, and then you took up a position at the Zenica Steel Works as a metalworker?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then you worked there until 1990?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1992, you joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH, in the 1st Zenica Detachment as an infantry man. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: By the end of 1993, you were appointed to administrative duties responsible for the distribution of mail within that unit?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And your duties primarily consisted of you delivering mail?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, in the spring of 1996, you became the chief of the general services section at the headquarters of the 7th Mechanised Brigade in Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was your role to act as the chief of administration which included mail distribution and archiving of documents?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Smriko. I'm going to now take you through your role as an archivist within this unit. What was the military system for the archiving of documents based on? What kind of instructions did you have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at the beginning, Ms. Benjamin, our learned colleague, said that the witness was just a clerk, not an archivist. So I don't see the purpose of asking such questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think if I can correct that, can I put it to the witness and ask him what exactly his role was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly what was your role in this unit of the 7th Mechanised Brigade in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: We have to make a difference between the role I had before 1996 and after 1996. It's necessary to make a distinction between the roles I had at these various periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Then, can you briefly tell us what was your role before 1996.

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Before 1996, my role was just to distribute documents, not to take care of the archives as well. These duties were performed by my predecessor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you tell us your duties after 1996.

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: When my predecessor left, I took over that job.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was that job? Can you please describe in greater detail what exactly was that job and what it entailed. What was your title, to begin with? Did you have another title then?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I was the dispatcher or courier up until 1996. And as of 1996, I was the chief of the office for general affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What was your duty -- what were your duties in relation to archiving documents, if any?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: As far as archiving is concerned, we would receive orders from our superior commands at the end of the calendar year. We didn't do anything on our own initiative. We would receive orders from our superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who would that superior command be?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: At the time, it was the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps command, did you say?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you know what system of archiving documents was used in the military at that time? Were you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: The system we followed was one based on temporary rules for handing over archival material. It had been issued by the BH Army General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did this archiving system follow some sort of methodology or formula as any other institution that you know?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I don't know about the system in force in other institutions. But it was quite explicitly stated how archival material should be collected and handed over to the relevant institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you have any instruction manual as to how you should approach the documentation and archiving?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already said, we followed the temporary rules that had been issued by the BH Army General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you given any formal training in this?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: No. I wasn't given any formal training. The instructions weren't complex, and it was possible to be in a position to follow them very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, how many people were in the staff of who were doing the same thing? Were you alone, or were there other people with you?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: There were three of us who worked there. But as of 1996, I was the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did it mean to be the "person in charge"? Were you somebody who would give orders to the other staff members?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I was the person in charge in the sense that the archival material had to be handed over to the relevant archives in time according to the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, what were you ordered to do when you got some documents? What were your instructions? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: We would draft our own order at the level of the brigade, and we would distribute it to our subordinate units so that they could follow the same order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you would draft your own orders, who would sign these orders?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: The brigade commander would sign them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would his deputy also sign?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: It was customary, if this was necessary, the commander to let his deputy sign documents if he was absent for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what would you do? How would you classify these documents when you got them?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: We followed the instructions in force at the time. And the documents were categorised. They were placed into five or six categories. For example, orders were placed in a separate category; analyses in a different category; reports in a third category. And there were certain other categories of documents different from the ones that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps this might be an appropriate time to break. I see the time is 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's 10.30. We'll have a break now. And we will resume at about 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you were telling Their Honours that you were categorising the documents in various general headings. Could you tell us, after you categorised the documents under these various headings, what would you then do with these documents?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: The documents were put in chronological order according to the date when they were drafted going from January through to December. And then they would be individually entered into a certain form which was called the archival list from the first to the last. And once this was done, space was left for a signature on the part of the persons who completed this part of the job. And it would be signed by the authorised person, and thereby it was felt that all the archival units, or rather, documents, had been entered into the archival list. And then it was possible to hand over the archived documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How was this done? Was this done electronically or was it done by hand?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: More recently, with the help of computers. But during the war, it was done by hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate date you started to computerise. Was it after 1996?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps in 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How would you actually select the documents? Would you select them in order of importance? Was there some criteria that you used?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: No. Only according to the temporary instructions issued by the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina documents would be classified into groups, not according to importance or weight. For instance, a group for reports, a group for analyses, a group for orders, a group for plans and so on. Without taking into consideration their importance or the weight they carried.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were these documents stamped as you archived them, as you gave them a number?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: For a document to be archived, it had to meet certain criteria. And those were that it should be signed by the authorised person and that there should be a stamp on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were you familiar with the kind of stamps which were used?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: There were changes over time in the stamps. If a unit changed its name, this automatically meant that the stamps would also have to be amended. And while I was working with stamps, I had to be familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were you also familiar with the various signatures of the commanders and the deputy commanders when you looked at them in the documents?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes. We had to be able to recognise the signature of our commander and other persons that he might authorise to sign on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How would you then -- would you be able to say after looking at any particular document that you received that it was authentic in the sense it was genuine?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Are you referring to the period in the past or now?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Tell us in the period in the past first, and then you can tell us now.

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Within the system of military correspondence, the office I was working in was one of the links in the chain of security to make sure that there should be no unauthorised use of stamps or signatures by persons who did not have the authorisation to do that. So we paid a great deal of attention to the authenticity and trustworthiness of both the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, this register, was it kept on an annual basis?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was this register, were you meant to transport the documents after one year, a week, a month, to the general archives?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: We acted at the end of the year, calendar year.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What would you do at the end of the calendar year?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: The rule was that an order would come from the superior command with detailed instructions, brief instructions, with reference to the book of rules that we have already referred to, that we should prepare the documents and complete the archival activities up to a certain deadline, and these deadlines were given to all the units; that is, the date by which they had to complete the work on the documents and hand over the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Where would they be handed over?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: In the case of my unit, we would hand over the complete archives to the 3rd Corps Command, which was our immediate superior unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And after you handed over to the 3rd Corps, you were ceased of the matter, or did you know what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Let me tell you briefly the actual technique of handing over documents between my unit and the corresponding archives of the 3rd Corps. When arriving in the 3rd Corps archive on the date scheduled for the handing over of documents, the authorised person from the command of the 3rd Corps who was authorised to take over the archives would check out the technical correctness of the archived material which was about to be handed over. He would, applying a certain methodology, in the spirit of the rules on the handing over of archives, he would check out certain things. And any incorrectly archived document would be sent back to the unit for completion; or if everything was in order, he would take over the archived material, and then an official note would be compiled with the signature of both the person handing over the material and the person taking over that archived material. Once the archives were handed over, the person who was fully responsible for its further use would be the person, the authorised person in the superior command, and that would be the end of my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At the time the documents were in your custody, could you tell us, please -- could you tell the Court, please, who would have access to these documents other than yourself and your staff?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I believe that during one calendar year, an order would be written, or rather instructions issued as to who was permitted to enter the archives, or rather to use the archives. And this was limited to a very small number of persons. Maybe the commander and his two assistants or something like that, in addition to my staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So only authorised personnel could come into your archives. And when they did come into your archives, did they have to sign any sort of register to say they had visited the archives and seen certain documents?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I don't remember during my duties there that anyone had ever taken any documents from the archives. If he would do that, it was envisaged that a receipt should be given or a report written, though I do not remember that anyone availed himself of this possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So they were, according to you, very secure while in your custody and control?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: My experience in these activities, which covers a number of years, shows that the commander carefully monitored and selected the persons he could entrust, stamps, documents, and archives, too. And it was a certain honour and a great responsibility for the persons chosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Indeed. Just one last question, now, Witness: What did you do with the documents which you didn't archive?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: There was a group of documents that could not be considered as archival material because they do not have the necessary significance. These were insignificant documents which don't have the need to be preserved for any length of time, and they would be destroyed, again, with a report being written. So destroyed legally. What I have in mind primarily are documents of lesser significance such as requests and other documents which didn't have any real significance and could not be treated as archival material because they weren't important.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before I end with you, Witness, can you please tell the Court, when you looked at a document, how would you authenticate it? How would you archive it? What would you look for in that document?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Of the greatest importance for us was that it should be signed and certified and that it was classified in the proper group.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would it also need a stamp?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was obligatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So a stamp, a signature, and certification; these are the three things you would look for?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: First the signature. That is the proper order. First the signature, and then the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would that be the seal? Would it be sealed as well?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What do you consider a stamp? What would you call the stamp, this stamp that you talk about on a document?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: A stamp and a seal. There were the reception stamps that were placed on documents reaching the unit which confirmed the date and the time when that document reached our unit. And the seals were round in shape, and they confirmed the authenticity of the signature of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there anything else you would look for in a particular document before you decided it was authentic?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: No. Nothing else that would be important for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you about your rules of archiving and the basic characteristics that you would look for. Sorry, can you please -- what I want to ask you is where would these rules come from which you utilised to do this work of yours?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly now, but as far as I can remember we used the rules taken over from the former Yugoslav People's Army that were slightly modified. But basically, it corresponds to the present methodology applied with documents. It hasn't changed substantially, the organisation of work when it comes to documents and seals.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And is it the same formula as the Federation of the BH Government is now using, the same kind of rules?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: When the joint command was formed of the army of the federation, a change occurred at the same time in the method of work applied in the offices of the administration. So we are using the instructions and rules and decrees which are currently in use by all the administrative organs of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina since 1999 so that we are now working on the basis of unified principles.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's all from this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I turn now to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Smriko. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic. You told my learned friend that ever since 1996, you had been working in the 7th Mechanised Brigade, which is the successor of the 7th Muslim Brigade, as chief of the general services office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that since 1993, you were working in the same service, but mostly as a dispatcher or courier of mail. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that some questions put to you were not quite clear to me, I wanted to ask you whether everything you have just said explaining how mail is registered, how lists are made for the archives, is that what you did after you became chief of this office? That is, after 1996, is that the procedure that you have now explained?

utterances.speaker: SABAHUDIN SMRIKO
utterances.text: Yes, that is the procedure, and it hasn't been changed to this day. We are using the same archive lists. The procedure slightly differs from what I just said because I indicated that certain changes were made, but not of any significance, once the joint commander of the federation was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that when you said that you received orders and instructions from your superior command, that is, the 3rd Corps, you were referring to the period when you took over the position of chief of the office.
